definition: "C" curve = pinch/active (compressed) anatomical shape; "S" curve = stretch/passive (elongated) shape.
Neck muscle that pulls the head forward and rotates it laterally; a baseball-bat shape from manubrium to base of skull.
Chest muscle pulling the arm forward and rotating it medially; a fan or goldfish-without-head shape on the rib cage.
Muscle rotating, lifting, and pulling the scapula; an upside-down dagger shape.
The three-headed shoulder muscle; an upside-down triangle from the side.
The abdominal group flexing the trunk at the lumbar vertebrae; a bullet shape with eight sections.
The side muscles bending the trunk laterally and twisting; two elongated rectangles supporting the rib cage over the pelvis.
Muscle sliding the scapula forward; an egg form with three tabs on the rib cage.
The muscle group (sacrospinalis) extending the vertebral column and head; two corn dogs side-by-side.
Back muscle adducting, extending, and rotating the humerus; a bowl with small triangular arms.
The animation technique of working sequentially from the first Keyframe to the last, drawing each in-between as you go, as opposed to planning Key Poses first.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: The animation technique of planning and drawing the extreme Key Poses first, then filling in the in-between Frames to connect them.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: A set of foundational animation guidelines (Squash and Stretch, Anticipation, Staging, Straight Ahead and Pose to Pose, Follow Through and Overlapping Action, Slow In and Slow Out, Arcs, Secondary Action, Timing, Exaggeration, Solid Drawing, Appeal) established by Disney animators.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: A Blender lamp type that simulates ambient illumination arriving from all directions, giving a uniform fill to the Scene (as of Blender 2.6x-2.7x).
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: A light property (as of Blender 2.6x-2.7x) that uses ray-tracing to compute shadow edges, producing sharper shadow boundaries than the default sampled shadow method.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: The rate at which a light's intensity, a Force Field's strength, or a proportional-editing influence diminishes with distance from its source.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: A category of Compositor nodes (Invert, Blur, Glare, etc.) that create or modify alpha mattes to control the transparency of composite layers.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: Per-field influence values on a particle system that control how strongly each Force Field (Wind, Gravity, etc.) acts on the particles.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: A particle constraint (as of Blender 2.6x-2.7x) that guides particles to follow along a Curve Object's path.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: A particle interaction model (as of Blender 2.6x-2.7x) computing short-range attraction and long-range repulsion between particles based on their distance, used for molecular-style simulation.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: A line-rendering feature (as of Blender 2.6x-2.7x) that produces stylized edge outlines over rendered geometry, separating it from the background.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: A render quality technique that reduces jagged staircase edges (aliasing) at object boundaries by sampling multiple points per pixel.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: Blender's built-in Python module providing programmatic access to all Blender data blocks, properties, and operators.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: A discrete Blender operation callable from the bpy.ops namespace (e.g. bpy.ops.mesh.primitive_cube_add), equivalent to a menu or panel command.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: Blender's Python module providing vector, matrix, and quaternion math utilities for scripting and add-on development.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: The Python API parameter (id(keyframe_insert=True) or .keyframe_insert()) that records an animation Keyframe on a property at the current frame.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: A Blender Add-on that toggles a Bone chain between Forward Kinematics and Inverse Kinematics control with a single click, simplifying the animation workflow.
source: Blender for Animation and Film-Based Production

definition: The number of Frames allotted to an action; slower timing (more Frames) reads as heavier or more deliberate, faster timing as lighter or snappier.
The distance an object travels between consecutive Keyframes; wider spacing reads as faster motion, tighter spacing as slower motion.
The principle that secondary parts of a body (hair, cloth, ears) continue moving slightly after the primary body has stopped, producing natural follow-through.
A preparatory movement in the opposite direction before the main action, alerting the viewer to what is about to happen (e.g. crouching before a jump).
The continued motion of secondary body parts after the main action has stopped (e.g. a character's coat swishing after a turn).
The natural curved paths that moving objects and body parts trace in space, as opposed to straight-line motion; following arcs produces more organic animation.
The rough, pose-by-pose pass of an animation where key positions are placed and checked for composition, timing, and readability before in-betweening.
A group of rough animation passes (blocking, overlap, follow-through) assembled and reviewed together before the final polish pass.
Matching a character's mouth Shape Keys to the phonemes of recorded dialogue so the mouth movement reads as speech.
A standard set of mouth Shape Keys (AA, EE, OH, OO, F, L, etc.) representing the main phoneme positions used for lip-sync animation.
A distinctive silhouette feature (e.g. a prominent nose, cape, or weapon) that makes a character instantly recognizable even as a small black shape.
A 360-degree rotation of a character model used to verify that the design reads clearly and consistently from all angles.
A Blender simulation type (Mantaflow, as of Blender 2.4x, 2.46) that models liquid flow, splashing, and interaction using domain-based solvers.
A Mantaflow domain simulation (as of Blender 2.4x, 2.46) that computes buoyant fire and smoke particles rising and dispersing through a fluid domain.
A particle-based hair and fur system (as of Blender 2.4x, 2.46) that grows individual curve strands from emitter surfaces to simulate hair or animal coats.
The group of scapular muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, teres major) that rotate the humerus and stabilize the shoulder.
Rotator cuff muscle that abducts the arm and helps stabilize the shoulder.
Rotator cuff muscle that laterally rotates the arm and helps stabilize the shoulder.
Rotator cuff muscle that laterally rotates the arm and weakly abducts it.
Rotator cuff muscle that adducts and medially rotates the arm.
Upper-arm muscle from about half-way down the humerus to the ulna, used to flex the forearm.
Upper-arm muscle from the top of the arm/shoulder to the radius, used to flex and supinate the forearm.
The three-headed (lateral, medial, long head) muscle that extends the arm at the elbow.
The forearm bone that rotates around the ulna; fat at the bottom, skinny at the top, on the thumb side of the wrist.
The static forearm bone, hinge-connected to the humerus; wider at the top, on the pinky-finger side of the wrist.
Rotation of the forearm in which the radius crosses over the ulna.
Rotation of the forearm in which the radius and ulna lie parallel; more powerful than pronation.
The three-muscle group on the medial half of the forearm, most active in gripping, making a fist, and pronation.
The ovoid muscle group on the back of the forearm, active in extending the wrist and stabilizing the elbow.
The two-muscle group on the outside of the forearm that aids in flexing the forearm at the elbow.
The arrangement of windows or panels displayed on the computer Screen when the program is in operation.
Blender is maintained by the Blender Foundation and released as Open Source Software, free to be used for any purpose.
The dedicated processor on the graphics card with its own RAM; renders faster than the CPU.
A designated area on the Computer Screen represented by an icon in the form of a button or bar, with or without text annotation.
The startup panel shown in the centre of the Screen on first launch, carrying Quick Setup options.
The default display Theme of Blender.
One of the GUI panels (3D Viewport, Outliner, Properties, Timeline); each has an Editor Icon for changing its type.
The two principal 3D Viewport working modes: build the Scene as a whole vs. model an Object; toggled with Tab.
The mesh elements: corner intersection points, the joining lines, and the areas they surround.
A basic mesh building block (one of Blender's ten basic shapes) from which modeling begins.
Blender's built-in monkey-head mesh, used as a test/benchmark model.
The scene point at which new Objects are placed and manipulations occur; distinct from the mouse cursor.
The lower-left panel that reports the most recent operation and lets you fine-tune its values.
The set of properties describing how an Object behaves under light; in its basic sense the color applied to an Object; a Blender datablock.
The cubic volume that bounds a physics (smoke/fire) simulation.
A recorded state of an Object (Location, Base Color, etc.) at a given Frame; Blender interpolates between them.
The portion of the Scene the Camera captures, and the only part that renders.
The arrangement of Editor panels for specific tasks; Blender's Editor-tabbed layouts (default Layout/General).
The cosmetic appearance of the interface (e.g. Blender Dark); installable as XML or created in-app.
The 3D Viewport panel (hidden by default, N key) for adjusting the selected Object's properties.
The 3D Viewport panel (T key) housing the Tools/Widgets for the selected Object.
The Properties Editor buttons (Output, Render, Scene, Object, Material, etc.) that gate different control sets.
The configuration panel for Blender's settings and Themes.
The 3D content (Objects, Characters, Lighting, Background) displayed against a background; the fundamental unit of a .blend file.
The two Viewport projection modes, toggled with Num Pad 5.
Blender's native file format; a package of data/elements that produces the on-screen display.
The trailing dot-name that tells the OS which application opens a file.
The in-Blender panel for navigating the computer's file system.
Take a copy of data (Objects, materials, cameras, etc.) from an existing .blend into the current file.
Reference data from another .blend so it stays in the original file and edits propagate.
Bring an external 3D file format (Collada, OBJ, DXF, etc.) into the Scene.
Embedding external data (textures, sounds) into the .blend for portability.
The image preview option in File Display Options.
The three Object-mode manipulations, each axis-lockable or numeric.
The on-Object colored handles (Move/Rotate/Scale/Transform) from the Tool Panel.
The Tool-Panel tool for linear and angular measurement.
Clay-like Objects that merge when brought close together.
The three engines that convert Blender 3D data into a 2D Image or Video file (Eevee the default).
A model whose surfaces are formed by a mesh of Vertices, Edges, and Faces.
The Header toggle that lets you see and select hidden geometry.
The operation that inserts new Vertices at Edge midpoints (Number of Cuts).
An Object's centre point about which rotation occurs; movable via Set Origin.
Merge Objects (Ctrl+J) or split them (P key: Selection / By Material / By Loose Parts).
A named set of Vertices that can be re-selected and manipulated as a unit; must match the Bone name for Armature control.
The brush tool for painting (graduated) weights onto Vertices to assign them to a group or Bone.
Change surrounding Vertices within an adjustable radius (Falloff Type) when editing one selection.
Create new Faces inside a selection (Thickness/Depth).
A relationship so Objects move together without joining (Ctrl+P).
Stretching a selection by duplicating and repositioning Vertices (optionally axis-constrained); for 3D Text, the Shape property giving depth.
The Tool-Panel tool (Widget) with Extrude to Cursor / Extrude Along Normal / Extrude Individual.
The tool/Modifier that bevels the Edges of a selected Face; for 3D Text, the Shape property rounding extruded edges.
The tool that creates new Edges and Edge Loops without selecting Vertices (Number of Cuts; Offset Edge Loop Cut).
The tool that cuts new Vertices and Edges by dragging.
The tool that creates Polygon Surfaces by clicking.
Rotating a selection about the 3D View Cursor; the cross-section line drawing spun to generate a solid (e.g. a wine glass).
Duplicating an Object around a circular path (default twelve; Steps).
The Modifier that supersedes the old Screw tool, producing a Screw effect.
Smooth rounds mesh corners; Randomize displaces Vertices randomly.

term: Edge Slide / Shrink Fatten / Shear / Rip Region
definition: Tools to slide an Edge, expand/shrink a selection, shear via a handle, and translate (rip) a selected Edge.
Pre-assembled code applying a process/algorithm to an Object; found in the Properties Editor Modifiers tab.
The two-stage workflow: Add the Modifier and adjust values, then Apply it to assign the data permanently (Object Mode only).
The ordered list of Modifiers on an Object; the top takes precedence and is reorderable.
The four categories of the Add Modifier menu: Modify / Generate / Deform / Physics.
A Generate-group Modifier that bevels the Edges of a Face.
A Generate-group Modifier that mirrors an Object, default on the X Axis.
A Generate-group Modifier that adds smoothness (Viewport/Render Levels).
A Deform-group Modifier deforming a primitive via Cast Type/Factor/Radius/Size.
A Deform-group Modifier displacing an Object or Vertex Group (Midlevel/Strength); used for Texture Displacement.
Modifiers that activate simulations (Particle System / Physics Simulation), auto-added to the stack.
Duplicating at Vertices; instancing an Object at each Vertex of a secondary Object via the Instancing tab.
The mode/workspace for adding surface detail by manipulating Mesh Vertices with a Brush.
The cursor circle (colored by Tool) and tool that pulls/pushes Vertices; effect set by Strength and Brush Radius.
The Header toggle that mirrors Sculpt deformation (or Bone duplication) about a centerline.
The Blender Add-on that automates landscape generation.
The surface pattern of a Material; together Material + Texture describe an Object's appearance.
The box on an Object that holds a Material's properties and name; an Object may hold multiple slots.
The tool for setting the Material Color (Diffuse) value via RGB/HSV/Hex.
The Viewport display modes and the option controlling whether the Material's response to light is shown.
The Editor that hosts node-based Materials (Noodle connections between node sockets).
The standard physically-based shading node (Base Color/Metallic/Roughness/Specular/IOR/Transmission/Alpha) whose Surface output feeds the Output node.
The panel/settings governing how color values are interpreted and displayed.
The curved connection lines in the Shader Editor that link node sockets to pass data.
The Add > Shader Node menu from which nodes are inserted.
The Layout Tab presenting the Shader Editor alongside the 3D Viewport.
Combining two colors/shaders with a Mix/Mix Shader node.
A node mapping a value across a color gradient.
The Mode painting per-vertex color into the Mesh to modulate a Material.
A Texture built into Blender, produced by code generating a pattern in accordance with mathematical formula (Brick, Magic, Voronoi).
The Node connected to the Principled BSDF Base Color socket that outputs a Texture to the surface.

term: Image as a Texture / Image Texture
definition: Loading an image (JPEG/BMP/PNG) as a Texture assigned in Material Properties Base Color, Mapped onto the surface.
How a 2D Texture is configured on the surface of a 3D Object.
Laying the Mesh surface flat (UV Editor); Unwrap options in the UV Editor Header UV Button.
A Texture workflow of Images (diffuse/normal/height/roughness) connected to the Principled BSDF to simulate surface lumps and bumps that react with light.

term: Texture Properties / Texture Channel / Texture Cache
definition: The Properties Editor panel acting as a Texture repository; Channels of Type Image or Movie; the Cache forms a per-file Texture Library.
Modifying a Mapped Texture by painting over it with a Material Color or another Texture.
Deforming the surface using the color shades of a Texture Image via the Displace Modifier, controlled by Midlevel/Strength.
A graphical representation of code processing blocks arranged/connected to produce effects.
Combining a Rendered Scene with saved Images/elements into a Composite Image.
The default Compositor Node Tree endpoints.
Nodes used to blend and fit a saved Image into the Rendered View.
The Editor for Node-based Texture painting in Brush Mode.
A Texture Node connected to an Output Node for Texture painting.

term: Geometry Node Editor / Geometry Node Workspace
definition: The Editor/Workspace for Geometry Nodes (Spreadsheet, 3D Viewport, GNE, Outliner, Properties).
The start/end of the Geometry Node Pipeline.

term: Transform / Point Instance / Point Scale Node
definition: Geometry Nodes for displacement and Vertex-based instancing.
The Material blend mode (with Screen Space Reflections/Refraction) that makes a Material display as transparent; used for text transparency.
Scattering light through a defined volume for beam, mist, and fog effects.
The volume Shader Node and its key value for Volumetric Lighting.
The illumination (Lights) that creates the mood of a Scene; effective only in Rendered Viewport Shading.
The four Light types set in the Light Tab.
The Object Data Properties tabs for the selected Camera (Lens, Depth of Field, Aperture, Safe Area, Background Image, Viewport Display).
Changing the active Camera during Animation via bound Markers.
The Timeline marker and Ctrl+B binding that drive Camera switching.
Imitating real Camera motion by plotting multiple video points onto the 3D Camera.
Using multiple Lights to create mood and control shadows.

term: World Background / HDRI Map / Environment Texture
definition: The ambient background light and high-dynamic-range Images that affect Material display.
Non-rendering tracing templates vs. rendering Image-Planes.
How the View in an Editor (the Viewport) is displayed.
Mesh display with see-through Mesh detail.
The default modeling display.
The three Solid lighting methods, independent of Scene Lamps.
The six Solid color types (Material, Single Color, Random Color, Texture Color, Vertex Color).
The three Solid background options (Theme, World, Viewport).
Object outlines (orange when selected) in Solid shading.
A preview of the final Render, lit by the Scene Lamps.

term: Material Preview / Scene Lighting / Scene World
definition: Quick preview under Lamp or HDRI/World illumination.
The World Properties background color affecting the Viewport.
Isolated display of Render passes (Combined, Diffuse Color, Normal).
The two Properties Editor button groups for Render and output settings.
The number of Render passes for quality.
The image size, shape, and playback settings (Resolution, Percentage, Aspect, Frame Start-End-Step, Frame Rate).
The save location and Image/Movie format selection.
Render > View Animation.
The routine that encodes the animation data for an output media.
Combining Clips and sound into a movie; distributed rendering of long sequences.
The illusion of motion, its captured Frames, and the time axis.
How Blender computes the in-between Frames.
The vertical blue line marking the current Frame.
Manually playing the animation by dragging the Cursor.
Auto-inserting Keyframes on Move/Scale/Rotate.
The per-channel display of animated data (green = data, orange = no data).
The Animation Editor with Show Sliders and per-channel controls.
The editable graphical display of the animation curves.
The curve and its manipulable points at Keyframes.
The list of animated actions in the Graph Editor.
A method of expressing 3D Rotation (global + local).
The vertical (Frames) and horizontal (units) blue lines.
One animatable parameter shown as an editable curve; includes Rotation and F-Curves beyond basic transforms.
The Graph Editor panel for a selected F-Curve.
A named collection of Keyframe data from multiple Objects/channels, controlled as one unit (Multi Object Keying Sets).
Driving animation Keyframes from an audio clip.
A dedicated larger animation workspace (preset Animation layout).
The Action/Constraint that drives an Object's movement along a Curve.
A non-renderable Object made of Bones that controls the movement of other Objects in animation.
The component of an Armature; has Tip, Body, Root; connected in a hierarchy.
An Armature with multiple Bones arranged to fit a Model for Posing/Animation.
The hierarchical link where a Child Bone follows its Parent Bone.
The Armature working Mode for Posing Bones (with Object/Edit Modes).
A Modifier that links a Mesh to an Armature (Bind To: Bone Envelope or Vertex Groups).
The volume around a Bone that determines which Vertices are controlled.
The menu (Ctrl+P) offering With Empty Groups / With Envelope Weights / With Automatic Weights.
A block of information (Mesh, Material, etc.) that generates a display in the 3D Viewport.
A free Open Source human character modeling program used to generate the demonstration model.
The Bone-duplication option that mirrors Bones to the opposite side of an Armature (with X-Axis Mirror).
A Bone Constraint that allows a single Control Bone to drive a chain of Bones (Target, Chain Length).
A Bone disconnected from the chain, used to manipulate the IK chain or Pose a limb.
The IK parameter determining how many Bones in the chain are affected (0 = all).
A Bone Constraint that forces an Armature to follow a Curve shape (Spline Fittings, Target).
A non-renderable 3D Cross object assigned to a Curve Control Handle for manipulation (Ctrl+H).
The process of creating an Armature for a Character Model and associating Bones with Mesh parts.
A mesh model with a minimum number of Vertices, Edges, and Faces.
The primary Control Bone for moving the entire Model in the Scene.
The Set Parent To option that auto-assigns Vertices to Vertex Groups.
The developed Control Bones (custom Object display) used for Posing a Character.
The animation of a Character walking on the spot, with the Base Control Handle following a Path.
The Blender Add-on (Rigging: Rigify) providing pre-assembled Armatures.
The toggle that excludes a Bone from mesh deformation (used for Control Bones).
A distinct Object type in Blender for creating text in the Scene.
The Blender Font slot in Object Data Properties; holds the font name and variants.
The four variants (Regular, Bold, Italic, Bold & Italic) selectable per Font.
A type of Curve used as a Path for text placement.
The Object Menu command that converts a Text Object to a Mesh Object.
The Object Menu command that converts a Text Object to a Curve Object.
The option for loading a specific font file (.ttf) into the Bfont slot.
The final assembled video output from combined Video Files; originated from Moving Pictures.
A pre-rendered animation clip (.avi format); the source material for the Movie.
A horizontal strip in the VSE where Video Files are placed; upper Channels take precedence.
A Video File in the VSE; can be cut (Soft/Hard) and modified.
A VSE cut where both segments retain data for the other part.
A VSE cut where data for the other part is not retained.
An audio file (.wav, MP3) added to the VSE to enhance the video.
A Modifier applied to a Video Strip in the VSE Properties (e.g. Color).
The .avi video codec used for the Movie output (no conversion from .avi source clips).
The TV frame-rate standard (25 frames per second) used for the Movie output.
A Text element added to the VSE for Title/credits.
The Blender editor that displays the Scene as a File Tree of Objects and Datablocks.
A named group of Objects arranged hierarchically like folders.
The default top-level Collection containing all Objects in the Scene.
The display of the Scene in the 3D Viewport; Collections are organized within this hierarchy.
The Outliner search/filter for finding Objects by name or type.
The eye/camera icons for hiding/showing Objects from Viewport/Render.
The Add-on Quick Effect that divides a Mesh into cell parts based on Point Source / Own Verts options.
A Generate-group Modifier that duplicates an Object in a grid, path, or object-offset array.
A Generate-group Modifier that cuts, unions, or intersects an Object with another (Difference/Union/Intersect).
A Generate-group Modifier that assembles an Object incrementally (per Face/Vertex/Edge) over an animation.
A Generate-group Modifier that reduces a Mesh Vertex/Edge/Face count by a Ratio (Collapse mode).
A Modifier that splits Vertices/Edges so selected geometry displays and renders independently.
A Modifier that limits an Object display to a region defined by a Vertex Group or a Mask Object.
A Generate-group Modifier adding scalable resolution levels to a Mesh, designed for use with the Sculpt Tool.
A Generate-group Modifier that recalculates how a Mesh Surface is constructed for shapes lacking detail geometry.
The Remesh detail parameter; 4 to 5 dramatically increases Vertices, 6 to 8 exponentially and slows the computer.
A Generate-group Modifier that gives a surface a Thickness (and optional Offset/Even Thickness).
A Generate-group Modifier that extrudes a mesh skeleton of Vertices and Edges into a solid surface.
A Generate-group Modifier ensuring consistent triangulation for rendering/export, placed above the Armature Modifier.
A Generate-group Modifier that merges close Vertices and welds seams, cleaning a Mesh surface.
A Generate-group Modifier that turns Faces into a wireframe of Edges with a set Thickness.
The Object Data Properties Normals option that cleans shading seams after Weld.
Pre-calculating and storing simulation or Render data to save time converting Viewport data into an Image or Video.
A deformable grid Object whose points can be moved to warp a parented or Lattice-modified Object.
A Deform-group Modifier that applies a Lattice Object deformation to the Mesh.
A Deform-group Modifier that deforms a Mesh to follow a Curve Object.
A Deform-group Modifier that snaps a Mesh onto the surface of a Target Object.
A Deform-group Modifier applying simple Twist/Bend/Taper deformations about an Axis.
A distinct Object type defined by a path of control points (Bezier/Path), not a Mesh of Faces.
The Curve Object Data property giving a Curve a 3D profile (extruded tube) along its path.
A rule that limits or drives an Object transform relative to itself or another Object (Object Constraints tab).
A Constraint making an Object follow the Parent Location/Rotation/Scale.
A Constraint that copies a Target Object Location, optionally inverted or offset.
A Constraint that aims an axis at a Target with a smooth Damped factor (vs. Track To snapping).
A Constraint forcing an Object axis to point at a Target Object.
A saved set of Vertex positions (Basis plus one or more shapes) blended by a Mix value to morph a Mesh.
The default 100% shape of a Shape Key set that all other keys are measured against.
A block of animation data (F-Curves, Keyframes) attached to an Object, editable in the Action/Dope Sheet editors.
A Modifier that emits, displays, and simulates particles (Physics Type) from an Emitter Object.
The setting controlling what renders for each particle (None/Halo/Mesh/Instance/Collection).
The initial speed and direction (Normal/Factor) of emitted particles.
A Particle System physics type simulating flocking/swarming behavior via Boid Brains.
The per-boid rule stack deciding how each boid steers (Separation/Alignment/Cohesion, Follow Leader, Goal).
The three core Boid Brain rules: avoid crowding, match neighbor headings, and steer toward the group center.
A Particle System physics type growing strands (Length, Interpolation, Children) from a Mesh surface.
The physics option making hair strands react (Spring, Damping, Stiffness) to forces and motion.
The particle physics mode migrating particles between Target Objects in sequence.
The simulation type where Objects collide and react under Newtonian Physics (Active/Passive, Mass).
The Rigid Body property type defining an Object collision shape (Mesh, Convex Hull, Cube/Sphere/Cylinder).
The Rigid Body option making an Object follow its animation while still colliding with dynamics.
An Object type (Wind, Gravity, Buoyancy, etc.) applying directional forces to physics simulations.
The simulation type modeling fabric (Stiffness, Tension, Compression, Shear, Damping) on a Mesh.
The cloth parameter resisting deformation (Bending/Tension/Compression/Shear sub-values).
The collision/physics parameter resisting sliding contact between surfaces.
The simulation type where a deformable Object (Pressure, Stiffness, Damping) reacts like a soft mass.
The stored simulation data (Cache Type Replay/Modular/All) written to a Cache Folder to free RAM.
Blenders fluid simulation engine for liquids and smoke/gas.
The Volume Object containing a fluid/smoke simulation, set to Flow type Domain.
The Flow type of a Fluid Object that continuously emits fluid (Geometry/Inflow behaviour).
The rendered surface of a liquid (Surface Thickness, Viscosity) inside the Domain.
The liquid surface effect (Foam/Threshold) creating bubbles at high-speed impact.
The system that paints (Surface/Generate) on a Mesh in real time as Objects pass over it.
The Dynamic Paint option masking where paint can be applied (by Object or Material).
A node in a Geometry Node Pipeline that processes geometry (points/edges/instances).
The Modifier attaching a Geometry Node Pipeline to an Object (non-destructive procedural geometry).
A Geometry Node (and Collision shape) wrapping geometry in the tightest convex Mesh.
A Geometry Node combining multiple geometry streams into one.
A Geometry Node that gathers the geometry data of another Object into the Pipeline.
A Geometry Node that converts a Curve (with profile) into a solid Mesh.
A Geometry Node instancing Objects (from Object Info) onto each Point in a collection.
A Geometry Node scattering Points over Faces (Density, Density Factor) for point-cloud/Field arrays.
A reusable, packaged 3D element (mesh, material, settings) placed in the Asset Browser and instantiated in the Scene, e.g. a Foliage Asset Pack.
A Geometry Node performing vector calculations (Add/Multiply/Sine) to shape arrays and Fields.
An expression (Driver Expression) that computes and drives a property value from other data.
The Non-Linear Animation Editor for layering, overlapping, and mixing Actions on Tracks.
A placed segment of an Action on an NLA Track, with adjustable Position, Scale, Fade, and Influence.
The fixed (0,0,0) point of the Scene, used as a reference for the 3D Cursor and Transform Pivot.
An invisible placeholder Object with no mesh data, used as a Parent, Constraint target, or transform controller.
The Ctrl+A operation that bakes an Object's Location/Rotation/Scale into its mesh so the values reset to defaults.
Modeling with Modifiers and tools that can be re-adjusted or removed without permanently altering the base mesh.
A mesh where every edge joins exactly two Faces (no holes or open boundaries), required for sculpting and simulation.
The deliberate arrangement of Edge Loops to follow a model's forms and support clean deformation.
The per-Edge/Vertex flag that forces a hard shading boundary (with Auto Smooth) to keep bevels crisp.
Small surface-detail features (panels, rivets, bolts) added to hard-surface models.
The modeling discipline for mechanical and industrial forms built from clean, flat quads.
The axis frame (Global/Local/Normal/Gimbal/View/Cursor) against which Object manipulations are measured.
The Sculpt option that adds and removes mesh density on the fly so detail follows the brush.
Rebuilding clean, low-poly topology over a high-detail sculpt for animation and export.
Sculpting at high resolution then baking that detail back onto a clean low-poly mesh for use.
A Sculpt brush that stretches and relaxes geometry like elastic.
A Sculpt brush that pulls a stroke into a coiled, snake-like shape.
A Sculpt brush that carves flat facets across multiple planes for a cut, gem-like look.
A Sculpt brush that adds material like sculpting clay to build up form.
The ratio of texture resolution to model surface area, kept uniform across a model to avoid uneven detail.
Texture dimensions sized to a power of two (512, 1024, 2048) for efficient GPU tiling and mipmapping.
The diffuse Base Color of a Material, its true color without lighting or reflection.
A map encoding surface normal detail to fake bumps and dents that react to light without added geometry.
A height-based map driving a Bump node to perturb shading without changing geometry.
The shading effect that darkens crevices where surfaces meet to suggest contact shadow.
The flat 2D (0-1) space where a mesh's UV Map is laid out for texturing.
A connected patch of unwrapped Faces laid flat in UV space.
An Edge marked to split the unwrap so the mesh lays flat without distortion.
Adjacent UVs sampling each other's texels at seams, corrected by UV padding.
The smart UV-project option that automatically generates UVs by angle and distance.
Scaling and arranging UV islands within the 0-1 space (with padding) to maximize texture use.
Pre-rendering (baking) a property (Diffuse/Normal/Roughness/AO) from a mesh into a texture.
The bake mode that transfers detail from a selected high-poly object onto the active low-poly's UVs.
A playback mode that runs the animation forward then backward before repeating.
The Timeline's final frame number (default 250) that bounds an animation's range.
Special visual effects (particles, physics, volumetrics) that are not solid-appearing meshes.
A cheaper effects technique animating a sequence of pre-drawn frames on a plane instead of heavy particles.
A stylized rendering style that deliberately departs from photorealism.
The Cycles Render option that removes noise grain from a render.
The unease produced by near-human but imperfect rendered characters.
A collage of reference images establishing the visual direction before production.
Illustrations exploring a project's look and feel before 3D production.
The enumerated set of meshes, textures, animations, and effects to build, used to divide work into milestones.
Roughly blocking a Scene with simple primitives to establish scale and composition before detailing.
A small but complete slice of the project (MVP) demonstrating the full pipeline end-to-end.
Lower-poly duplicates swapped in at runtime based on distance from the camera to save performance.
The rough, parent-first assembly of a model's major parts that establishes its overall proportions and silhouette before any detailing.
The hard-surface technique of starting from a cube/primitive and shaping it with loop cuts and edge/face moves rather than building up from many small pieces.
The book's term for expanding a face loop along its normals with Alt+S to give a flat loop thickness (distinct from the Solidify Modifier).
The movable 3D anchor that sets new objects' spawn point and, set as the Transform Pivot, drives snapping, scaling, and mirroring about it.
The built-in add-on (W menu) providing Circle, Relax, and Space tools that round or evenly space a selection of edges/vertices.
The transform tool (T > Shear) that slants a selected surface, with the offset value adjusted in the Shear menu.
A camera imaging artifact of light fringing outward from very bright areas.
Localized bloom-like blurring around angled highlights of a reflected light source.
The distance between the farthest and nearest in-focus objects; shallow depth of field directs attention.

term: Camera To View (Lock Camera to View)
definition: Setting the camera to the current viewport (Ctrl+Shift+0) or locking it to the view while you orbit.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: The dark border and frame around the render in the viewport/compositor that previews the final image area.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: The camera aperture value that controls the amount of depth-of-field blur in EEVEE.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: The two EEVEE Bloom parameters: Threshold sets how bright an area must be to bloom, Intensity sets how much it spreads.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: Gurney's illustrated science-fantasy world (a sunken continent) used throughout the book as a running example of applied color and light.
Fitting the full color space (color solid) into the limited gamut a painter's actual pigments can produce.
The practice of applying realistic observation of light and color to invented or fantastical subjects and worlds.
Applying small, discrete dabs of distinct hues that read as a mixed color at a distance, increasing perceived light and vibrancy.

A darkened enclosure with a small aperture or lens projecting an inverted image of the outside scene, associated with Vermeer; in animation layout, the device that first inspired artists to "draw with light", used as a full-circle metaphor for the evolution of layout.
source: Color and Light; Setting the Scene

definition: Painting outdoors directly from the natural scene, made practical by the 1841 portable paint tube.
A thin, transparent layer of paint over a dried underpainting so the lower layer's light modifies the upper color.
The mid-19th-century American landscape movement (Cole, Church, Durand) known for grand, luminous, carefully valued views.
The British movement (Millais and others) noted for direct observation and luminous glazing over an underpainting.
Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source (1/4 at 2x, 1/9 at 3x).
The unit of total visible light output (luminous flux) of a source.
Determined by the apparent size of the source; small sharp source = hard light and sharp shadows, large area (diffuser, shade) = soft.
The color cast of a light on the Kelvin scale; low values warm/orange, high values cool/blue.
A graph of how a source's energy is distributed across wavelengths, determining its perceived color.
Light from a heated tungsten filament; warm, continuous spectrum strong in orange/red, weak in blue.
Light from an excited gas; spiky spectrum, typically yellow-green, making outdoor daylight look violet by comparison.
A monochromatic, sickly orange street-lamp light.
A cool, bluish street-lamp light that flattens and cools skin tones.
Light produced by a chemical reaction in living organisms (fireflies, fish, squid, algae, foxfire).
Light re-emitted by a material after it absorbs ultraviolet radiation, seen in amber, calcite, some minerals.
Light produced by heat (a glowing filament or ember), distinct from luminescence.
A light whose origin is implied rather than shown, placed outside the frame, visible, or concealed to build mystery.
Light on a smooth matte solid produces an orderly, predictable sequence of value steps (lit side, highlight, terminator, core shadow).
Conditions (direct sun vs. overcast, source size, angle) that change the sharpness and range of the value steps without removing them.
A perceptual effect where context cues override raw luminance, making equal patches read as different values.
The brightness ratio of the lit side to the shadow side (from film); about two stops equals five value steps.
A mental exercise to see that even the darkest shadow is filled with light, by imagining an observer at ground level looking up.
A setup where a form is lit on one half with the rest in shadow, for drama (cf. the existing half-light entry).
Light from in front at about 45 degrees, illuminating both eyes; the most common portrait setup.
A portrait setup producing a small triangle of light on the shadowed cheek.
A setup where the larger side of the face is turned toward the light.
A setup where the smaller side of the face is turned toward the light.
The main light source in a lighting setup.
An additional source that raises the shadow side and lowers contrast.
Light from the viewer's direction, with very little shadow, emphasizing two-dimensional design.
Light from behind that grazes the side of a form, producing a rim light / kicker (cf. edge/rim light).
Backlighting where the subject stands before a bright sky or doorway, blocking the light and silhouetting the front.
Light from underneath (footlights, firelight), reading as magical or ominous because faces are normally lit from above.
In shadow, upward-facing planes read cool (blue, sky) and downward-facing planes read warm (ground).
Theatrical concentration of light on a single form to fix attention.
The small highlights in the eyes used in classical cinema to give a figure life and focus.
The attribute that distinguishes a color as red, yellow, green, blue, etc., independent of lightness or intensity.
The grayness or intensity of a hue; how far a color is from a neutral gray.
The purity of a light or color, the degree to which it is free of white or gray.
The lightness or darkness of a color relative to a neutral gray; the third dimension of the color solid.
The three-dimensional model of hue, chroma, and value (color solid) in which every color has a position.
Albert Munsell's objective system locating a color by hue, chroma, and value (e.g., YR 7/2).
The value at which a given hue reaches maximum chroma (yellow light, blue dark, red middle).
Two hues directly opposite on the wheel that neutralize toward gray when mixed, or heighten each other by juxtaposition.
Cyan, magenta, yellow - the secondary complements of RGB and the primaries of subtractive color in printing.
Red, green, blue - the primaries of additive light; mixing them yields white.
Newton's seven spectral colors (red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet).
The historical red-yellow-blue wheel with secondaries at the midpoints, criticized for uneven spacing and weak secondaries.
Gurney's universal wheel with six evenly spaced primaries (yellow, red, magenta, blue, cyan, green).
The color of a surface seen up close in white light, as a swatch held against it.
The low-chroma grays that are the artist's best friend and the "sauce" of a scheme; there is no single gray.
A high-chroma yellow-green, the electric color of new spring leaves.
Stapleton Kearns's technique of weaving a pink/reddish gray into greens to warm and vary them.
A smooth, glissando-like transition in hue, light-dark, or dull-saturated.
A hue mixed with white (a pastel), or a thin transparent layer over white yielding high chroma.
The colored solid that gives paint its hue and, suspended in a binder, its body.
The medium that suspends the pigment and binds it to the support.
The stable international identifier for a pigment (e.g., PB29, PR83) that appears on the tube.
A luminous blue, historically ground from lapis lazuli and now synthesized (PB29).
The ancient murex-shell dye, used here to illustrate a beautiful but fugitive, era-defining color.
A colorant that dissolves (rather than being suspended), many of which are fugitive.
A pigment's resistance to fading under light.
The American Society for Testing and Materials lightfastness scale, ASTM I (best) to III (fades).
A color that fades or shifts under light, unsuitable for work meant to last.
A pigment's full-strength color straight from the tube.
The color a pigment shows when thinned or glazed, often differing from its masstone.
The power of a small amount of pigment to color a large amount of another; a strong tinter.
Organic pigments tend to be transparent with strong tinting strength; inorganic ones tend to be opaque and chalky.
A toned ground (imprimatura) laid over the prepared surface before the final paint.
The sky painted first to set the tonal and color key of the picture.
Wiping a passage with a rag and a little medium to lower value or saturation.
Painting the final image wet-in-wet in one sitting.
A small, compatible set of pigments used to keep color relations under control.
Color that has gone flat and neutral from overmixing complementary hues.
Gurney's term for a palette that has gone gray and dead from too many mixed greens.
A color scheme built from value or chroma variations of a single hue.
A painting or underpainting executed in gray tones.
The mixing of colored lights, including the blending of colors in the eye rather than the mixing of pigments.
With two differently colored light sources on one form, the cast shadow of each source takes on the color of the other source.
A color scheme of three primaries whose gamut is a triangle.
A small area of color that stands out from the rest of the composition, usually by being complementary or more intense in chroma.
The two psychological color families: warm (orange, yellow, red) evokes fire and energy; cool (blue-green, blue, violet) evokes sky, shadow, and rest.
A series of prepared paint mixtures stepping a color note through values or chroma, laid out on the palette in order.
The practice of making paint mixtures as needed during the painting process; also called the open palette.
The practice of preparing organized paint mixtures on the palette in advance of painting; also called setting a palette.
The full range of color notes mixable from a given set of primaries; also the region of the color wheel that represents that range.
The inevitable loss of chroma produced by mixing colors of different hues.
A shape (e.g. a triangle) laid over the color wheel to visualize and rotate the limits of a scheme's gamut.
A color scheme based on a triangular gamut that does not include neutral gray.
A gamut shape defined by a pair of complementary hues, used as a mask to limit a color scheme.

In sequential media (books, film), the planning of the limited color range within each sequence and the transitions between them; in animation, the complete color script built from colored key sketches (thumbnails drawn on script pages) that establishes the film's color plan, with an abstract color-continuity script developed afterward.
source: Color and Light; Imaginative Realism; Dream Worlds

definition: Hues that are adjacent to one another along the outer edge of the color wheel; naturally related and harmonious.
The three (or more) starting colors chosen for a color scheme; they define its gamut and may be any hues at any chroma.
The color note at the geometric center of a gamut; unlike a chroma-matched gray it is shifted toward a hue and acts as the scheme's color cast.
A person with color blindness, especially the inability to distinguish red from green.
A person (or bird, insect) with four kinds of color receptors; some can respond to ultraviolet or infrared light.
A person with normal human vision, having three kinds of color receptors.
Retinal receptors: rods are sensitive to low light but cannot discriminate color; cones handle color and fine detail.
In very dim light, the rods (most sensitive to bluish wavelengths) cause greenish or bluish hues to appear lighter in value.
A theory of vision holding that perceived colors result from interactions of red/green, blue/yellow, and black/white (brightness) signals.
The perception of stability of local color despite changes in the overall color cast of the illumination.
The effect of an afterimage on the experience of a currently viewed subject.
The phenomenon in which a color appears to change due to the effect of an adjacent color.
The tendency of the visual system to adjust to a given color of illumination.
The brain's two visual streams: the dorsal "where" stream (motion, spatial, action) and ventral "what" stream (object and color recognition).
Light that has passed diffusely through a thin, translucent material, sometimes becoming richly colored.
The complexion zones of a light-skinned face: golden forehead, reddish mid-face, bluish or greenish lower third.
Reflection or refraction of light by curved glass or water, projecting spots, arcs, or bands of light onto other surfaces.
The mirror-like behavior of shiny objects, reflecting light rays at the same relative angle they approached.
A reflection of the light source on a wet or shiny surface, defining sets of parallel planes on the form.
Light reflected irregularly from an uneven surface, as opposed to specular reflection.
Patterns of small specular highlights forming concentric rings around a light source or a principal highlight.
A region of brightly colored light surrounding an intense light source, such as a setting sun or streetlight, akin to a lens flare.
Softening of edges that occurs when a form moves rapidly in front of a stationary camera.
Softening of edges that occurs when the camera tracks along with a fast-moving object, blurring the background along the path.
In photography, loss of information because the photosensor cannot respond to relatively bright or dim light levels.
Scattering by small air molecules of more short (blue) than long (red) wavelengths, producing the blue color of the sky.
The sky gradation governed by proximity to the sun; the sky lightens and warms toward the sun.
The sky gradation that depends on angle above the horizon; the sky generally lightens toward the horizon.
A device (or set of paint swatches) for evaluating and matching sky colors.
The part of a clear sky that is the darkest and purest blue, roughly 65-95 degrees from the sun.
The point in the sky or below the horizon 180 degrees from the sun, at the center of a rainbow's arc.
Progression of color from cooler colors in the foreground to warmer colors in the background.
The light qualities of the first and last hours of the day, including the effects of sunrise, sunset, and twilight; also called magic hour.
Horizontal bands of color that form low in the sky at sunset; usually orange near the horizon and blue above.
A shadow cast by clouds, contrails, or tree branches appearing as a darker shaft within a region of illuminated air.
A patchwork of circular or elliptical spots of light caused by sunlight passing through small openings in an overhead canopy.
Patches of shade drifting across a landscape as clouds interrupt the sun; useful for directing the viewer's attention.
Openings or apertures within the silhouette of a tree through which the light of the sky is visible.
The relatively darker region between the primary and secondary rainbows.
Faint rainbows that form at angles of less than 42 degrees inside the primary rainbow.
Water's selective absorption of wavelengths: red mostly absorbed by 10 feet, orange and yellow by 25, leaving a blue cast with depth.
The creation of multiple plein-air studies of the same subject under different lighting, or closely related studies made one after another, like frames of a film.
A render setting that makes the background transparent (alpha) in the output so the scene can be composited over another image.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: Fabric on the figure; studied through gravity-driven gesture, fabric character, and the seven folds tied to tension points.
A landmark renamed to relate it to the push or grab of fabric; imagined as a large, moveable wire hanger.
The fold where drapery ends; it always just fits to a wrapping line on the perspective of the form it conforms to.
The fold from a consistent placement of tension points, making the fabric look like cylinders lined up next to one another (shower/window curtains).
The fold caused by drapery suspended between two main tension points, designed with "C" and "S" curves.
The fold that takes place between any two tension points close enough to pinch fabric between them (e.g. the bend of the arm or leg).
The fold from two tension points twisting the fabric in opposing directions, ending behind the forms in a "T" overlap.
The fold remembering the asymmetrical compression of clothing from gravity and excess fabric, most likely seen at the bottom of the pants/leg.
The only fold showing external influence (wind, movement, flying); a "U" fold with an external element acting on it.
The group that, after the finished animation, approves rough and final animation as well as the color combinations; the production designer is a member.
A booklet of approximately 60 pages created after the green light, explaining the basic rules of the style for the departments Layout, Background, Animation, Effects, Clean-up and Color.
The moment a production is approved and the new project is announced to the outside world.
A matte used on characters so they do not blend into the background; *Mulan* executives wanted more of them, and Bacher cites *Lady and the Tramp* (without them) as not looking cheap.
Big foreground elements framing the action so all background perspective lines lead toward the characters, as in the *Cinderella* scenes.
A composition placement alternative to "closer to the edge" when deciding where to place the action in a frame.
Camera-position choices: shooting from below looking up (scary up-shots in horror films) or from above looking down.
Stills printed from taped TV programs (from the early nineties, via VHS/Laserdisc/DVD), Bacher's main medium for building reference archives of thousands of images.

An architectural-style sketch of the environments of a chosen sequence, marking the main light sources with arrows, character positions, and their movements; used for studying film and for complex camera moves.
A timed presentation reel of the story; the London team finished a ~50-minute color story reel for *Beauty and the Beast* in a very short time (early fall 1989).
The first timed test reel in Bacher's production timeline, later defined after sound recording and with elements exchanged.
Mostly French painting of Middle Eastern themes from around the end of the nineteenth century (favorites: Jacques Majorelle, Jean-Leon Gerome); the main reference for the *Aladdin* world.
The miniature painting tradition Bacher studied for the styling of the *Aladdin* palace garden.
Crossing the 180° invisible line connecting the characters; shots are allowed only along that line, and losing control of the logical sequence can "completely destroy a sequence."
A dialogue-scene camera position among the careful-planning tools (close-ups to medium-/wide shots, over-the-shoulder or POV).

The balance of wider shots versus close-ups and of character counts within shots; compared when analyzing movies, planned to keep budgets down, and — connected across scenes — the movie's visual language.
A slightly tilted camera angle that indicates something disturbing might happen; one of the tension-building tools of a climax.

The simple translation of a floor plan with actor positions and camera angle into a three-quarter perspective view, used to check character combinations before animation; Bacher's simplified version stayed 2-D.

The perspective-grid solution for closer shots where a character's contact to ground level is not visible: place the foreground character in the same size relation next to the background character and follow the grid to find the contact point.
External artists invited "from all over the world" to add ingredients for a unique look (e.g. Alex Nino, Regis Loisel, Vink, Harald Siepermann for *Mulan*).
A very old painting technique: a dry badger brush softens the edges of freshly applied color on cardboard; taught by Ric Sluiter and used to define the final *Mulan* background style.

The philosophy of balance everywhere in the Chinese landscape washes — detail as texture, more detail toward the foreground in stylized blossoms, bamboo and grass — that Bacher wanted to see in *Mulan*.

The "old traditional-style watercolor art from the beautiful Silly Symphonies" (*Elmer Elephant*, *Farmyard Symphony*, *Three Little Wolves*) that *Lilo & Stitch* recreated via the top background team in Florida; the style also studied for *Mulan*.
chapter: Ch 13 Lilo and Stitch (PDF 136); Ch 11 Mulan (PDF 122)

definition: The planned progression of color across a film's story events, parallel to the "emotion/action curve"; the "clear 'color-curve'" visible throughout *Lady and the Tramp* and *Sleeping Beauty*.

Sequences "designed in 'color-chapters'" with "color-transitions" between them, normally smooth or deliberately contrasting to indicate dramatic story changes, as in *Bambi*'s late-summer-to-first-snow scenes.
The point where a production is handed over/ended under new leadership — *Wild Life* "went into turnaround" while the team still hoped the story would be fixed.
Bill Peet's crosshatching for texture reimagined by Umesh Shukla as a "3-D crosshatched world" for the shelved *My Peoples* look, rejected as "too spiky" with an "artificial technical feel."
The "some thousand different brushes" Bacher designed for the flat textured look of *Fraidy Cat*, which "became an obsession over the years."
One of the decision meetings a production designer attends — "Story, workbook, brain trust, layout, back-ground, color, effects and sweatbox meetings."
Blender's real-time render engine that rasterizes (rather than ray-traces) lights and materials so a frame is produced while you work; the book's focus.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: Producing a viewable image continuously at interactive frame rate (as opposed to batch/offline rendering); the defining property of EEVEE.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A node that passes the shader output straight to the render result, bypassing the lighting model, used here to build stylized non-physical materials.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A Light Path node output exposing the current ray's pass, used so a shader differs for the camera pass versus reflection/refraction passes.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A Grease Pencil-based modifier (in development in Blender 2.93) that generates an animated line-art outline of a mesh.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: The EEVEE volume block (Start/End, Tile Size, Samples, Distribution) that controls how volumetric light is rendered and sampled.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A material/EEVEE setting (e.g. "None") controlling whether a transparent material casts shadows.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: An artifact where light bleeds through thin geometry in a rasterized engine; mitigated in the book with Solidify and render-setting tweaks.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: An EEVEE render setting that raises the internal bit depth to reduce shadow and gradient banding.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: An EEVEE shadow setting controlling how the shadow map is split into cascades (sharpness versus artifact).
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: The aim of making a rendered 3D scene read as a real photograph; the book's governing goal for the cabin and landscape projects.
Using actual measured dimensions (Metric units in Blender) for objects instead of estimating size by eye.
Replicating the exact camera position, rotation, and focal length of a reference photograph so the 3D scene matches it.
The camera lens parameter (mm) that fSpy recovers from a reference photo and the user tweaks to match the reference framing.
The texture channel holding a material's surface color, connected to the Principled BSDF Base Color socket.
The black-and-white channel (set Non-Color) controlling reflection: black = shiny, white = rough.
A Blender procedural node (used at scale 5 and 50) to generate layered wood-like detail.
A Blender procedural node added to break up the CG-perfect look of a surface.
The Principled BSDF value (raised, e.g. to 0.9) that makes a surface read as metal.
Saving the UV map as an image to paint on in an external texture editor.
A free Blender procedural texture of white and dark spots, used as the driver for the Displace modifier.
The UV-mapping option (U menu) that unwraps the mesh as it appears in the current viewport view.
The particle Render As Object setting that replaces hair particles with a chosen object (a plant).
The particle Render setting (default 0) that randomizes the size of scattered particles.
The particle Rotation setting (Velocity/Hair to Global Y) controlling the upright orientation of scattered plants.
The shading command (right-click) that smooths a mesh's surface shading so its edges are not flat-faceted.
The Shader Editor node (e.g. Bright -0.2) used to make texture colors more vivid before Base Color.
The Compositor node that places one image over another using alpha to fill transparent render areas.
The Compositor node that previews the running composite result.
The underlying noise basis selected in the A.N.T. Landscape add-on (default Blender, changed to Voronoi F2) that shapes the procedural terrain.
The Shader Editor node exposing geometric data (e.g. the Normal output), used here to encode surface orientation as RGB.
The shader node that splits a vector into its X, Y, and Z components to isolate a single axis.
The Edit Mode operator (Ctrl + E) that fills a gap between two selected edge loops.
The shader node that refracts and reflects light passing through a surface, used here for water's reflectivity.
The shader node that adds transparency without refraction, passing light straight through the surface.
A measure of how much a light ray bends passing from one medium to another (water is 1.33).
The Timeline F-Modifier that loops an animation.
The Material > Settings 'Surface' mode (Displacement and Bump) that enables real displacement alongside bump, requiring Cycles.
The Shader Editor node that groups and labels related nodes to organize a setup.
The Ctrl + G operation that packs a node tree into a single, reusable group node exposing only essential parameters.
A grayscale texture that determines where and to what degree two materials mix on the same object.
The UV unwrap method (U in Edit Mode) that projects the mesh as if it were a cube.
Using a black-and-white mask in the Principled BSDF Alpha slot so only the masked area renders and the background becomes transparent.
One of the two Particle System configurations (as of Blender 3.3); the default type, not used for scattering in this book.
Particle copies (Simple) that reuse parent geometry to raise visible density at low computational cost (as of Blender 3.3).
The render control that stops rendering after a set duration (e.g. 5 minutes).
A Cycles node setup (Bevel + Geometry + Vector Math Dot Product + Invert) that detects sharp edges and renders them white on a black model.
The image (Bake Type Emit) baked from an Edge Mask and used to drive edge wear on a surface.
The worn, darker-or-brighter-edged look produced from an edge map via a Mix + Power + ColorRamp node chain.
The shader node (Samples, Radius) that simulates rounded edge bevels for edge detection and normal-map baking.
The Cycles Selected-to-Active bake that turns a high-poly pattern into a normal map image.
The normal map baked from duplicated, beveled edges to fake smooth bevels without added polygon count.
Painting transparent PNG stickers onto a surface via Stencil mapping in the Texture Paint Workspace.
A baked normal-map sticker painted onto a surface to fake modeled detail without geometry.
The Cycles bake of a small model into a normal map for use as a paintable decal.
The line framework of the figure, considered the foundation for everything planned; like an armature to a sculpture or a rig to a 3D model.
One of the only three line types; used for active, pinched, compressed forms.
One of the only three line types; used for stretched, passive forms and for the spine.
The third permitted line type, used for direction and length; a straight line drawn across a form is avoided in favor of wrapping lines.
Head, spine, rib cage, pelvis, two arms, and two legs - the parts described in a gesture drawing.
Offsetting curve apexes so the eye moves through the design; the main line use in gesture drawing.
Repeating a similar curve or shape twice or more, which provokes visual movement.
Controlling the speed of the viewer's eye (fast vs. slow areas) through line combinations.
A volumetric contour that travels around a form to indicate perspective, like a rubber band tied around it.
The figure's balance line; exaggerated out of balance to create dynamic poses.
A mid-action position that suspends the outcome of the action, engaging the viewer's anticipation.
Using as little line as possible to describe the differences between muscle, fat, and bone.
Katzenberg's label for the book: a complete practical manual of the visual language of storytelling.
The rules and techniques of the image medium that must be understood before personal style can be explored.
The Introduction's prioritization method: general intensity of the image, then narrative detail, then artistic execution and style.
The fictional world a storyteller creates on paper that the audience must experience as real.
The book's term for the techniques and rules that translate perceived mood into a drawing.
Foreshadowing or hinting rather than spelling things out, so the audience fills in the gaps.
The main tool for creating a world of parallel reality, based on lighting, pacing, and color.
Coherent visual and emotional choices from the first to the last frame, established by the first shots.
Drawing with masses of light and dark; contour lines do not exist in reality and can be dropped when they get in the way.
Prioritizing and highlighting certain elements in a composition based on what is required at the moment.
Off-center composition based on the thirds grid lines or their intersections, preferred over regular symmetry.
Accidental touchings or coincidences between elements that look premeditated and pull the audience out of the story.
The culturally familiar reading direction; action moving with it reads as positive, against it as difficulty.
The point where lines parallel to the horizon converge, toward which parallel lines recede in a perspective construction; an obvious center of interest that attracts the eye.
A lens that includes a wider view and exaggerates depth clues and perspective distortion.
A lens that focuses on a narrower portion, minimizing depth clues and flattening the image.
With 35-mm film, the approximate equivalent of the undistorted human-eye view.
