A wall covered with clippings and sketches used by a theme park design team to generate and narrow ideas.
A rough physical model, similar to a maquette, used to define how people will flow through a themed attraction.
The broader field of themed, place-based experiences that includes theme parks, hotels, casinos, and themed retail establishments.
Areas of bone that visibly push through the flesh (clavicles, sternum, iliac crest, etc.), giving the figure the feel of an active skeleton.
The line down the center of the skeleton; a "C" curve when rib cage and pelvis face the same way, an "S" curve when twisting.
One line clearly passing in front of or behind another, the main tool for showing recession and depth.
Flesh compressed where two bone areas move toward each other, shown with a "C" curve.
Elongation where two bone areas move apart, shown with an "S" curve.
The bone resembling bicycle handlebars that acts as a lever for arm movement.
The bone fusing the rib cage in the front; with the manubrium resembles a neck tie.
The free-floating bone that guides and aids the movement of the arms.
The top of the femur, a landmark at the hip used to locate the leg's placement.
The perspectival unit of clavicle (front) and scapula (back) sitting on the rib cage; moves independently and organizes the shoulders.
The shapes surrounding the figure, designed through limited, curve-based line use (fluid/rhythmic on the passive side, jagged on the pinched side).
Moving the leg away from the body; the abductor muscle shapes are compressed during this movement.
Moving the leg toward the body; the opposing movement to abduction in the leg's muscle design.
Hip muscle originating under the iliac crest that abducts and medially rotates the thigh; represented as an ellipse.
Hip muscle represented as a triangle, very similar to the shape of the deltoid.
Muscle involved in both adduction and abduction; simplified as a butterfly shape.
Hip muscles whose primary shape is a triangle with the base along the back of the femur and the tip toward the pubic bone.
Band on the side of the leg; a point of insertion for the tensor fascia, sitting over the vastus lateralis and inserting into the tibia; a wrench-grabbing-the-femur shape.
Muscle flexing the lower leg and rotating it medially; a long "S" curve from the iliac crest to the inside of the tibia.
The three large back-of-leg muscles (semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris) flexing the knee; an ellipse with two tendon legs.
The four-muscle group on the front of the femur (vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, rectus femoris, vastus intermedius) flexing the hip and extending the knee; a large ellipse.
Calf muscle, grouped with the gastrocnemius, raising the heel and preventing the figure from falling forward.
Calf muscle, grouped with the soleus; origin at the fibula, inserting into the calcaneus/heel block.
The heel block into which the calf muscle inserts; a cube in the foot's structural design.
The more square/block-like bottom that the large calf ellipse trails into.
The natural principle that a form is designed to match its needed function, illustrated by the foot's support/weight-absorption design.
The front-to-back arch of the foot (example A), built in the structural design as a bridge forward in space.
The side-to-side arch of the foot (example B).
The largest bone collection of the foot (roughly half the foot), reduced in the structural design to a sphere and the heel cube.
The mid-foot bone group connecting the tarsus to the ground plane; designed as a box built from an "S" curve, similar to a slide.
The set of light conditions with the edges used to integrate them, diagrammed in the closing chapter.
The rule that a change in value on the figure describes a change in surface, in exactly the same way as a wrapping line.
Light whose rays are aligned in a singular direction, casting hard-edged shadows.
Diffuse light from many points, casting soft-edged shadows.
A light source at a finite distance whose rays fan out (contrast with sunlight).
The diminishing of light strength with distance from its source (a.k.a. falloff).
Shadow cast where two adjoining surfaces meet and block light.
The darkest part of a cast shadow where a form meets a surface or in cavities.
Back light illuminating only an object's edge to strengthen its silhouette.
Lighting in which only half an object or scene is illuminated.
Light bouncing off one surface to illuminate another (a.k.a. bounced/fill light).
Illuminated atmospheric shafts / edges of cloud shadows.
Reduced value contrast and saturation with distance.
The shadow a form projects onto another surface.
The line where the light side transitions to the shadow side (where light rays are tangent).
The dark band of gradation starting at the terminator on the shadow side.
The brightest area of a matte surface, fixed relative to the light source.
The reflection of the light source, which moves with the viewer.
Value change that speeds up near the core shadow rather than running linear.
The angle at which light rays strike a surface, governing its value (a.k.a. light ray angle).
The color-temperature scale (e.g. 5500 K for daylight) used to set realistic natural lighting.
The node that converts a Kelvin color-temperature value into an RGB color for a light's Color socket.
The World node that adds procedural sky lighting with its own sun (Sun Size, Sun Intensity, Elevation, Altitude, Air, Dust, Ozone).
The compositing node that adjusts the render's color/values (Gain) to change its mood.
The compositing node that adds lens flares/glows (e.g. Fog Glow) around bright areas.
A light's emitted energy (watts) controlling its brightness, the primary knob for light strength.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: An area light's physical size; larger gives softer shadows, smaller gives harder shadows.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: An EEVEE light probe that captures indirect/ambient (irradiance) light from the environment to improve shading accuracy.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: The probe action that bakes the scene's indirect light (and optionally the cubemap) into a probe for reuse.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: The behavior of light on a surface; the subject of the book's second half.
Reflection strength grows stronger as the surface rolls away from the line of sight (weakest at perpendicular, strongest at tangent); chrome is 100% shiny from any angle.
The brain reads light values as mostly matte and dark values as mostly reflective; contrast between reflection and base paint makes a surface look shinier.
The environment appearing upside down on a shiny concave surface because the reflecting sight lines invert it.
Floating-island reflections caused by reflection flipping, often melting into one continuous perimeter.
A sight line bouncing off one reflective surface onto another and then to a different part of the environment, changing the reflected color.
The transparent reflective layer over a base paint (or carbon weave) that carries the environment's reflections.
An airbrushed layer mask that fades reflections where the line of sight is perpendicular, creating the Fresnel Effect.
The sky's own value change - darkest straight up, lightest at the horizon (dust, smog, moisture) - that chrome reflects directly.
A base coat of tiny floating mirrors (flakes) at different angles that scatter sight lines back to the light source from a wider area, intensifying the light reflection.
Softly expanding or lightening a base coat toward the light source's color to simulate metallic reflection.
Light penetrating a translucent material and scattering within it, creating a glowing effect.
The change of direction of a ray of light, distorting what appears behind glass.
Surfaces that glow and emit their own light, taking no cast shadows.
Uneven reflection from aligned microscopic scratches (brushed/machined metal), like tiny aligned cylindrical cross sections.
EEVEE's real-time reflection technique that approximates reflections from the already-rendered screen buffer (no ray tracing), central to the water scene.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A small helper object that captures light (reflections or irradiance) from its surroundings and feeds it to a material or the scene.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A plane used as a reflection light probe that captures the environment for a local reflective surface.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A shader node that outputs the Fresnel term (edge-on reflectivity) to drive a material's edge reflections, as in the water material.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A baked cube-map probe that supplies accurate, static reflections to a region (as opposed to live SSR).
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A probe bake option that stores only the reflection cubemap (not irradiance) for a probe.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: Applying value, color, and light/shadow to a drawing so volumes read as three-dimensional.
A non-reflective surface; the focus of the book's first half.
Three clearly differentiated surface values (lightest, mid, darkest) that make a volume read as three-dimensional.
The value of an object's physical color, independent of lighting.
The span from the lightest to the darkest value used on an object.
The inherent value of a color/material independent of lighting.
Rule: shadow-side/cast-shadow value = (10 − true value) ÷ 2.
The general surrounding light that fills shadows.
A simple geometric volume (box, cylinder, cone, sphere) used as a rendering foundation.
A compound form defined in a three-axis perspective coordinate system.
A surface bending in only one direction; the building block of X-Y-Z forms.
A line on a manufactured object that separates panels and reads like a section line (a.k.a. panel/part/shut line).
The physical roughness of a surface, shown by value changes.
The reduction in visible detail with distance, giving depth perception.
A constant value appearing to shift value depending on the surrounding background.
The appearance of top lighting created by a background/value gradation.
The lightest value in a rendering, which must be darkened for saturated colors.
The principle that a color's value must be set before colorizing; saturated colors are far darker than intuition suggests.
Converting a scene into a 2D image by projecting and shading primitives (EEVEE's method) as opposed to ray tracing.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A render technique that simulates light by tracing rays from the camera and their bounces through the scene (Cycles' method).
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A material/shading model built on physically plausible light behavior, shared by both EEVEE and Cycles.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: The contribution of light that has bounced once or more between surfaces, as opposed to direct light.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A material whose surface color/texture comes from an image texture (as opposed to procedural generation).
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A shader that makes a surface emit its own light/color independent of scene lighting.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A procedural texture node generating cell-like patterns, used here for smoke and rock detail.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: Deliberately bypassing physically based shading to produce stylized, artistic looks (as in the Stylized Scene project).
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A procedural texture node that produces a smooth one-axis gradient, used for fake clouds and mist.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A compositor/material node that remaps color channels by curve for grading and contrast.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A compositor node that saves (or exports) the composite or an individual pass to a file.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A node that adjusts Hue, Saturation, and Value (brightness) of an image independently.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: The compositor feature showing the scene (or a saved render) behind the node graph for reference.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: Storing an image's color already multiplied by its alpha, as Blender imports detail/alpha images by default.
source: Shading, Lighting, and Rendering with Blender EEVEE

definition: A texturing technique that stores surface-normal information in a texture to simulate fine geometric detail (bumps, engravings) without adding actual geometry.
A Compositor node that applies directional motion blur using a Vector (velocity) pass, as opposed to the simpler fixed-direction Blur node.
A render pass (Vector pass) that outputs per-pixel motion vectors (X, Y, Z displacement) for use in post-compositing effects like vector blur or camera shake.
The tonal range between the darkest and brightest values in an image; increasing contrast pushes midtones toward black or white, decreasing it compresses them toward gray.
The middle range of luminance values in an image (between highlights and shadows); adjusting midtones shifts the overall brightness without clipping the extremes.
The default, unposed state of every Bone in an Armature as it was built in Edit Mode; the reference from which all deformation is measured.
The Armature pose at which a Mesh is first skinned to it; the starting state used to compute vertex deformation.
Named collections of Vertices on a Mesh, each with a per-Vertex weight (0-1), used to control how much a Bone influences each Vertex.
The process of assigning Mesh Vertices to Bones (via Vertex Groups and weights) so that deforming the Bones deforms the Mesh.
A Bone-constraint method in which the position of a target (effector) is set and the solver works backward to orient each Bone in the chain, used for arms and legs.
The default Bone-control method in which each Bone in a chain is rotated individually from the root outward; simpler to animate but harder for multi-Bone chains.
The 2.4x-era IK mode (as of Blender 2.4x, 2.46) that automatically adjusts Bone chain lengths to reach the target, as opposed to the later iterative solver.
An IK chain that has no explicit target Bone; the end Bone itself is the control point, simplifying the rig by one control.
A simplified copy of a character Armature used for fast blocking or as a lightweight control layer, keeping the full-rig file separate.
A non-renderable control object (Empty, Curve, or Mesh) that drives a deformation via a Lattice, Mesh Deform, or Armature Modifier without being rendered.
A non-renderable object (typically an Empty) used purely to position, orient, or drive another object or Bone; never appears in the final render.
The per-Vertex values (0 to 1) in a Vertex Group that determine how strongly a given Bone influences each Vertex during skinning.
A Modifier (as of Blender 2.4x, 2.46) that deforms a Mesh based on the deformation of a target Mesh object, used for proportional or surface-driven deformations.
Shape Keys on a character head representing discrete expressions (smile, brow raise, jaw open) that can be blended by Mix values to build a face.
Individual Shape Key components (e.g. one eye, one brow) that are combined (additively) to build a full expression, as opposed to whole-face Shape Keys.
A technique (as of Blender 2.4x, 2.46) where the eyes are modeled as spheres with a Lattice or proportional-edit deformation to produce a natural rolling motion.
The object constraint that maps one object's location, rotation, or scale to another's, used here to drive tank tracks and wheels from a single empty sphere.
The department and craft that frames the performance, plans camera moves, and dictates the cost of every shot before animation begins.
The total amount of line drawing a production requires; TV animation does not reduce it despite simpler style.
Framing a set-up to a specific field (aspect ratio/format), shown as fielding diagrams.
A framing guide drawn on the layout indicating the required field and safe area for the shot.
A set field (format) that the camera does not change, as used on lathe beds.
A field that is photographed at an angle, with maximum tilt limits that vary by field size.
A background designed to move (pan) through the platen, usually pegged to the top.
A camera move that dollies toward or away from the scene within the artwork.
An East-West (sideways) pan, one of the basic camera moves available on a fixed camera.
Overlay and underlay: drawing one element over (or under) another to create depth or a cutaway.
The bar holding the peg holes that register every sheet and background in the camera.
Peg holes on the sides of a background used to shift it sideways (for pans) without changing the top/bottom registration.
Peg holes that allow a sheet to be shifted a fixed, known distance.
A peg bar that registers a background for a pan, often with side pegs.
The flat glass plate in the animation camera on which the stacked sheets and background sit.
A transparent sheet bearing a single drawing (usually one character/part) in a stack.
An object or prop that persists across a scene (e.g. cars, a family unit), painted by Ink-and-Paint rather than the BG department.
An animation camera that photographs cels at different heights to create true depth/parallax.
The improved multiplane camera design that could vary the number and spacing of planes.
The downward-facing camera in the animation camera that photographs the platen stack.

Predigital frame-image compositing technique (per the book's glossary) involving the photography of both "solid" and projected elements â€” the latter being an "aerial" image because the beam of the projected image does not "land" on a solid surface; often used to combine live-action footage with animation.
The working document (X-sheet) that records every shot's drawings, cels, sound, and timing.
The clean red line marking where animation must register to the background.
The Walt Disney Studio's multiplane camera, coyly described by that name in U.S. Patent 2,198,006 (designed by William E. Garity).
A support that holds a drawing (or background) for the camera, associated with fixed fields.
A line or shape used to mask/define an area, e.g. a matte line separating overlapping elements.
A camera that photographs a set-up at an angle ("setback") to suggest depth.
A rough photographed test of drawings against the background to check the shot before clean-up.
A test reel of posed character drawings bridging storyboard and character layout.
An individual rough panel or group of drawings from the board, used before it settles into a linear storyboard.
A device that projects film onto a drawing surface so poses can be traced.
A reference grid used to check and build perspective/depth in a layout.
A deliberate, non-literal shortcut used to suggest depth or scale.
The framing that keeps all essential action within the portion of the image domestic TV sets displayed.
The width-to-height proportion of the image frame; a sequence cannot be staged identically in two very different ratios.
Wide-screen formats whose aspect ratios push composition and framing choices.
Disney's in-house digital ink-and-paint and computerized image-compositing system, another Academy Award winner that led the field in both areas.
The effect when a repeat pan background is too short, so the same elements reappear too quickly behind the characters.
"Same as" / "works out of": a scene based on previous material, with re-used animation xeroxed into the folder.
The required amount of drawings an artist must produce; a reality even in feature work.
The upstream planning of a shot (framing, moves, edits) that layout commits before animation.

A musical percussion cue (or cues) in Hanna-Barbera series such as *The Flintstones*, in which a rapid pattern of bongo beats accompanies a cycle of a character's feet running in midair before contacting the ground, at which point the character exits ("zips out") the scene.

The Academy Award-winning software package/process developed for *Tarzan* (1999) by Disney's in-house CGI team, allowing many of the film's environments to be modeled in 3D even though the character animation was hand-drawn.
Small physical sets/models used to give real depth and reference to a layout.
A background/lay-out shaped to fit a corner of the frame, leaving room for a move.
The name Tex Avery's unit gave to its temporary Warner Bros. accommodation; a catch-all for the Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies shorts.
The layout discipline of framing character gags with the minimum of scenic invention, prioritizing legibility, timing, and economy over cinematic elaboration.
A recurring cartoon environment (e.g. the *Road Runner* desert) that operates as a quasi-character, establishing finite parameters within which the comedy is staged.
The group of young CalArts graduates mentored by Maurice Noble at Chuck Jones Productions in the late 1990s.
A colored drawing showing the intended color design for a shot or sequence, used as a guide for BG painters.
The Warner Bros. practice of drawing background layouts after the character animation was complete, so the scenic design could reference the actual performance.
The per-film production documents recording every shot's timing, camera moves, background requirements, and cost implications.

A path-of-movement curve designated by Scene Planning for a camera move (per Bill Perkins, art directing on *Aladdin*), whose mathematics layout duplicated in the final composite for blurs, lighting changes, and the like.
A precision camera (on a rostrum table) that photographs artwork in multiple passes/exposures, used for multi-layer integration.
The technique of photographing multiple layers (character cels, effects, backgrounds) in separate passes to build a single composite image.
The specific shape of the flat background painting for the *Who Framed Roger Rabbit* kitchen sequence, designed for extreme perspective shifts.
Jeffrey Katzenberg's term for the 2D/3D hybrid: hand-drawn animation inhabiting a 3D computer-modeled environment.
The technique of painting scenic artwork and projecting it onto digital planes to create an illusion of depth and scale.
The ability of computer tools to move the camera along the depth (z) axis as well as the traditional x and y axes.
The department/role at CG and VFX studios responsible for planning camera moves, framing, and environmental staging for live-action/CG hybrid shots.

The practice (per MacLean) of isolating an area within a background painting or set model at a key narrative point so a lead character can declare something important to the story â€” e.g. the miniature "proscenium" built for Cruella de Vil in *The Dalmatians*.

The ch. 08 principle that characters get into cars or go to the kitchen only because the story requires it; writers, directors, and designers establish a plausible context from the outset (exemplar: MGM's *Tom and Jerry* kitchen).

Maurice Noble's concept, as told by Pixar's Scott Morse: "He thought about design itself as texture"; Ernie Nordli's *Incredibles* design echoes it; in CG production language, "texture" usually refers to the rendering of surface detail.
The description of CG character animation as the manipulation of a pre-built model in 3D space, analogous to physical puppet traditions.
Ray Aragon's core teaching philosophy: the layout artist's eye is the camera, and the artist must learn to position, move, and frame as a camera would.
Aragon's insistence that layout is fundamentally about composition ("Set it up! Stage it!"), not the mechanical process of drawing backgrounds.
Aragon's description of the 1950s-60s Disney animation community: a collaborative, friendly culture unique in the world of commercial design.
A page marker indicating the section is about observing reality.
A page marker indicating the reader should apply the steps to make their own work.
Pencil-holding method useful for adding lines and details.
Pencil-holding method for loose concepts and smooth gradations.
Rendering media that do not fade or blur over time.
Paper/board that prevents added media from degrading.
A blend mode used to overlay a line drawing or cast shadow without hiding underlying values.
A digital layer setting so edits affect only existing pixels, preserving edges.
The deliberate staging of light direction to feature the best of a subject.
A constant-angle tangent used to find common value points on a curved surface.
A growing, categorized collection of only the best photographs of materials, lighting, and reflectivity phenomena, used to inform new renderings.
Using a Mac/iPhone Photo Booth mirror filter on found objects (crumpled paper, a wooden post) to generate alien character faces.
Starting a digital rendering from a photograph and painting over it in Photoshop as an auxiliary drawing tool.
Modeling in a 3D program (e.g. MODO), outputting a base rendering, then adding lighting, detail, form refinements, and atmosphere with 2D skills (e.g. Photoshop).
The free, open-source program that estimates a photo's camera parameters (focal length, position, rotation) from its vanishing points and exports them into Blender.
The built-in add-on enabling one-click PBR texture setup (Ctrl + Shift + T) and node preview (Ctrl + Shift + left-click).
The built-in add-on (part of Add Mesh: Extra Objects) used to generate rocks in one click.
The larger add-on (Gears, Pipe Joints, Rock Generator) containing the Rock Generator, enabled from Preferences.
The Node Wrangler action (Ctrl + Shift + T) that wires a PBR texture set into the Principled BSDF by matching file-name keywords.
The Blender editor that tabulates Geometry Nodes data (points, elements, attributes) as editable rows and columns, used to inspect and filter node data.

definition: A modeling operation that cannot be tweaked after the transform is finalized, revertible only by Ctrl + Z.
A face with four edges and four vertices, technically two combined triangles, the basis of a clean quad-based workflow.
A plane of connected quads, the perfect topology for a flat surface.
A continuous line of edges through a row of connected faces whose flow is checked with the Loop Cut tool.
A vertex where more than four edges meet, formed at the corners where two grids intersect, usually kept to five edges or fewer.
The direction a face points, determining how light bounces off the surface; all normals on a mesh should face the same direction.
The operation (A, then M, then By Distance) that merges coincident or near-coincident vertices to remove duplicate geometry.
The viewport option that snaps a selection to an edge, face, vertex, or volume, used here to faces to align vertices.
(1) loops terminate into the void or themselves, (2) loops do not intersect themselves, (3) loops do not spiral down a mesh.
The bending or stretching of a finished mesh (any shifting of the mesh), as driven by an armature or a physics simulation.
Rule 1 - the edges of the grid must be parallel to the axis of deformation.
Rule 2 - the axis of twisting should be in line with the edge flow.
The twisting failure caused by too little geometry to distribute the twist, fixed by adding geometry.
Rule 3 - keep a buffer of at least one row of faces between a pole and the area of deformation.
The Physics modifier that gives a mesh a cloth simulation.
A Subdivision modifier setting that adds geometry without smoothing the mesh.
An image texture that can be laid next to itself with no visible seams, requiring the UV map to unwrap into a clean plane.
The UV-editor Overlays option that visualizes per-face warping (blue/green/red) to judge unwrap quality.
The UV-editor option that shows the full map and syncs selections between the 3D Viewport and the UV Editor.
The three first checks - all faces are quads, no duplicate geometry, and all face normals oriented the same direction - that must be met before the other rules can be checked.
The shape-based rules (loops terminate into themselves or the void, do not overlap, do not spiral) that direct how topology is laid out on a mesh.
The rules (grid edges parallel to the axis of deformation, twist axis in line with the edge flow, one row of faces between a pole and the deforming area) that ensure good deformations.
A string of vertices/edges laid along a detail or across an area to mark the path faces should follow before the area is filled in.
The behavior where a loop cut placed between two snapped ends inherits a shape that blends from one end toward the other, so loops read like whichever snapped end they are closest to.
The shading mode that shows the normals exactly as shown by the geometry, with each face separated by a sharp edge.
The shading mode that averages the normals of intersecting faces to smooth out their edges, which can create shading artifacts on sharp corners.
Anything that causes the final surface of a model to look off, here caused by smoothing corners that are too sharp.
The operation (double-tap G) that slides a vertex along the edges it is connected to, used to pull and merge unnecessary loops.
The setting (Active Tool and Workspace) that merges vertices within a set distance, used with vertex slide to collapse geometry.
The number of triangles a mesh renders as (labeled Tris in Scene Statistics), the metric being reduced to improve performance.
The Status Bar view (right-click the footer) that reports the scene's triangle count and other statistics.
A face with more than four sides, produced when unneeded flat-surface edges are dissolved; tolerated in hard-surface work but avoided where deformation is needed.
